questionText:

"Ibn Battuta was fascinated by plants that were completely unfamiliar to his North African audience. Describing the coconut, he wrote: 'These trees are among the most peculiar trees in the world... The nut of a coconut tree resembles a human head, for in it are what look like two eyes and a mouth, and inside, when it is green, there is what looks like brains, and within it which is like hair. They make from this cordage with which they sew up ships instead of iron nails.' Describing the betel (paan), he noted: 'The betel is a tree which is cultivated in the same manner as the grape-vine... The betel has no fruit and is grown only for the sake of its leaves... The manner of its use is that before eating it one takes the areca nut, which is like a nutmeg, breaks it into small pellets and puts these in his mouth and chews them. questionText:

Assertion (A): According to Ibn Battuta, news from Sindh reached Sultan Muhammad bin Tughlaq in Delhi in just five days via the postal system.
Reason (R): The foot-post (dawa) was exceptionally swift because runners stationed at every third of a mile sprinted at top speed holding a rod with copper bells to warn the next runner.

3. Reason (R) correctly explains Assertion (A).

questionText:

"Francois Bernier left a harrowing eyewitness account of the practice of Sati which he witnessed firsthand at Lahore: 'At Lahore I saw a most beautiful young widow, not more than twelve years of age, sacrificed. The poor little creature appeared more dead than alive when she approached the dreadful pit; the agony of her mind cannot be described; she trembled and wept bitterly; but three or four of the Brahmanas, assisted by an old woman who held her under the arm, forced the unhappy victim toward the pyre, seated her upon the wood, tied her hands and feet lest she should run away, and in that situation the innocent creature was burnt alive.
